newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China may issue sugar tolling licences-traders.
newsitem.headline: China may issue sugar tolling licences-traders.

text.p: China may soon issue between 100,000 and 200,000 tonnes worth of tolling licences for sugar but relatively high raw prices and lower white sugar prices could make tolling less profitable, traders said on Wednesday.
Talk that China may issue between 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes worth of tolling sugar licences within the next two or three weeks circulated widely in Hong Kong and China's sugar markets.
"No formal announcements have been made, but we are hopeful," said a senior China-based trader by telephone.
In tolling, raw material is imported duty-free if the processed goods are destined for exports.
Most of the licences would likely be allotted to a major Chinese state-owned trading firm, sugar traders said.
"I belive that China will have to import July/September quarters," one sugar trader said.
Traders noted that weak white sugar prices and relatively firm raw prices would slash tolling profits and healthy sugar supplies in Asia would make Chinese sugar difficult to market.
A 26,000-tonne cargo of Australian sugar was awaiting discharge at a port in south China's Guangzhou city and anticipated the issue of tolling licences, sources said.
Japanese trade houses bought two cargos (24,000 tonnes each) of Thai raw sugar for July shipment at around 60-65 U.S. cents, Tokyo traders said.
South Korea purchased about three or four cargoes of Thai raw sugar, they noted.
A south China sugar refinery which imported sugar last month had sorted out documentation difficulties, most likely by extending the date on old tolling licences, sources said.
"It has all been sorted out," one sugar trader noted.
Thai raw sugar premiums have firmed on shortcovering sparked by the possibility of floods reducing the Thai sugar crop, Tokyo traders said.
Although Thai sugar output for this crop year was originally forecast at around 6.3 million tonnes, the market now expected the output at around 5.8 million tonnes, Japanese traders said.
"Japanese and South Korean buyers are stepping up (activity) in the market, triggered by views that Thai output may be lower," one Tokyo source said.
Market talk that Brazil could be unwilling to export sugar, also helped lift sentiment, the traders said.

"Given good demand for alcoholic beverages in Brazil, Brazilian traders may be more willing to sell sugar in the country, rather than exporting sugar. The factor also supported sentiment here," a source said.

Thai raw sugar premiums for April/May deliveries were quoted at 0.40/0.50 U.S. cents per pound (bid/offer) over New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) May futures on a FOB basis, compared with 0.30/0.40 U.S. cents a week ago.

May/July deliveries were quoted at 0.40/0.50 U.S. cents, compared with 0.35/0.40 cents a week ago. July/September deliveries were quoted firmer at 0.60/0.70 U.S. cents, compared with 0.50/0.60 a week ago.
Japanese traders said they were likely to continue buying Thai raw sugar, noting they wanted to buy before premiums jumped, in the event that China entered the market.
But Hong Kong traders said any leaps in July/September premiums would be capped on the upside, since Chinese buying would be limited.
